tagline: Concrete arches and railroad rails carry an earlier highway’s story
intro: The Black Hills Back Country Byway, also known as Old Safford Road, crosses the Gila River on two reinforced-concrete arches. The nearby Black Gap Bridge uses a different construction: railroad rails reinforce a short concrete span. The Black Hills form a mountain block that sends the Gila northwest, west and southwest.

Plans for the Gila crossing changed when steel proved scarce during World War I and bids exceeded the budget. Prison laborers built its two equal Luten arches in 1918. Black Gap followed in 1920–21, completing the Clifton-Solomonville Highway; US 666 later drew away most of its traffic. The state engineer designed Black Gap’s rail-reinforced span, a construction type used only for short crossings. The old crossing remained on a county route for local traffic.

Begin at Clifton on the San Francisco River, then head toward the Gila River Bridge and Black Gap Bridge southwest of town. At the Gila crossing, Owl Creek Campground occupies a cliff overlooking the bridge.

moments.title: Clifton
moments.text: Clifton stands along the San Francisco River and serves as the seat of Greenlee County. It was one of the places involved in Arizona’s copper mine strike of 1983. US 191 and the Arizona Eastern Railway serve the town.

moments.title: Gila River Bridge
moments.text: The Gila River Bridge went through three designs before its concrete arches took shape. In 1917, state engineer Thomas Haddock planned a higher, longer steel crossing, but high bids and wartime steel shortages ended that proposal. An open-spandrel concrete arch design followed. Then state engineer B. M. Atwood required two equal Luten arches at a lower, shorter crossing. Prison laborers built that version in 1918 for $60,191. The Luten design takes its name from Daniel B. Luten, who created the arch form. It continues to carry byway traffic, with Owl Creek Campground on the cliff above.
moments.notice: Two reinforced-concrete arches span the Gila River.

moments.title: Black Gap Bridge
moments.text: Railroad rails do the reinforcing inside Black Gap Bridge’s concrete slab, spaced 24 inches apart on center. This single-span bridge was built in 1920–21, the last link completed in the Clifton-Solomonville Highway across Greenlee and Graham counties. The state engineer designed this short-span type, whose reinforcement is built into the slab. It is one of Arizona’s few surviving bridges built by prison laborers. Also called Pumroy Canyon Bridge, it became part of a quieter route when US 666 took most of the traffic away. The crossing remains on a county route serving local traffic.
